subsequent_commits.message:
Bump zhong-hong-hvac to 1.0.19

discovery_ac() opened its socket before applying the timeout it was given,
and connect() takes its bound from the same place every other socket
operation does. An address with nothing behind it therefore ran to thirty
seconds however small a budget the caller asked for, which is exactly the
case a config flow needs answered quickly.

- Library diff: https://github.com/crhan/ZhongHongHVAC/compare/v1.0.18...v1.0.19
- Release notes: https://github.com/crhan/ZhongHongHVAC/releases/tag/v1.0.19

Leave the ZhongHong socket to the library

The config flow opened a socket of its own before discovering, so that a
mistyped address was answered for in seconds rather than at the pace of a
discovery that had not been bounded where it mattered. That is the
library's business, and 1.0.19 does it: the timeout now covers connecting,
so discovery alone reports an address with nothing behind it just as fast.

BREAKS_IN_HA_VERSION moves to const.py, since the import step needs it too.

Leave the ZhongHong entity naming to a later PR

has_entity_name, the device registry entry and the translation key for the
two fan speeds climate has no name of its own for are all worth having, and
none of them is what migrating to a config entry is about. They come back
together, with the tests that go with them.

The entity keeps a name of its own in the meantime, as it had before.

Connect to the ZhongHong gateway in one executor job

Discovery and starting the listener both block and have to happen in that
order, so they were two jobs with a trip back to the event loop in between
that had nothing to do while it waited. They are one job now.

Tell the user when ZhongHong YAML cannot be imported

The import created a configuration entry without contacting the gateway,
on the grounds that it takes one connection at a time and could still be
holding the previous run's, so a check would fail for reasons that say
nothing about the configuration.

That reasoning covers a gateway that is temporarily busy, and not one that
has been replaced or taken away, which the YAML has no way of knowing about.
Both ended the same way: an entry that never works. The gateway is now
contacted, and a repair issue names which part no longer holds instead.

Only ask for the YAML to be removed once it has been imported

The notice that a YAML configuration has been imported asks the user to
delete it. It was raised whatever the import did, so a gateway that no
longer answers got both that notice and the repair issue naming what had
failed -- and following the first would have left the integration with
nothing at all, the YAML gone and no entry to replace it.

Which issue to raise is now decided in one place, from what the flow
returned, the way the other imports in core do it. The config flow goes
back to aborting with a reason and no side effect of its own.

Keep the coordinator for a follow-up PR

The migration to a config entry does not need one. The gateway pushes
every change on its own socket, so the entities take their state the way
they did under the YAML platform, and what this PR is actually about --
where the connection lives, which entry owns which entity, importing the
YAML -- is unaffected by who schedules the updates.

So the coordinator goes out, and with it the three things only it could
offer: polling as a fallback for pushes missed while the connection was
down, availability derived from that poll, and the re-read a few seconds
after a command for the reports that never arrive. Those come back
together in the PR after this one, where they can be reviewed as the
change they are.

The entry still asks the gateway for the state of every unit once, when
it is set up. Without it the entities would sit unknown until somebody
touched a unit, since the gateway reports a unit only when it changes.
